doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Artists who never believed they had played it right
summary: Rollins, Wes Montgomery and Bill Evans kept wanting another take, and the producer has to say enough.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: about it, in which if not for me and the record company that I was operating and the way in which we proceeded with things — certainly a lot of careers would not have happened in the same way. I’m not saying that it wouldn’t have happened, but knowing what I do about — I’ll tell you, knowing what I do about some of the personalities that I dealt with I still haven’t figured out whether it was just luck of the draw or whether this is a more prevalent attitude than anybody appreciates but I sure have had a run of artists who never really believed that they have played it right. Who have to do another take because they didn’t get it yet, they haven’t done the best that they can do. And it’s amazing, I mean it’s a perfectly good description of Rollins, of Wes Montgomery, of Bill Evans. That’s a pretty good round up there. We used to have a standing joke about the creation, for recording purposes of a demon band, which would be made up of all of these people who never believed that they had done anything properly. There were a number of other people who I didn’t necessarily work much with directly but who were in the same category, J.J. Johnson, Percy Heath, a lot of people. And we were going to form this dream band as it were, there were two problems. One is obviously with that band you would never get an acceptable take on even one tune, and secondly you wouldn’t be able to find a drummer for that band. Drummers do not suffer from this problem. But other than that, that’s one of the major characteristics of jazz in my time anyhow. Well among other things, I mean somebody’s got to say hey, enough of this, let’s quit crapping around and go on to the next tune. Or, take my word for it, I really think we’ve got it there. One or the other of those takes has got it and we can always edit, but believe me let’s go on. And frequently the musician has no choice but to believe you, and so—
